findings.F1: Over 783 trades, those held 5 days or less lost on average (−6.2% net, 1.2% winners, for 244 trades of ≤1.5 days; −6.5% net, 6.7% winners, for 539 trades of 1.5–5 days), while the 204 trades held over 60 days made +60.7% net with 75% winners, so the book's gain comes from a few long holds and short stays above the average are mostly whipsaws.
findings.F2: After a large down day the next day rises more often than usual: 58.6% of next-day excess returns are positive after a day below −2.5 trailing 20-day standard deviations (n=268, mean +0.66%, t=1.67), and 59.6% after a day between −2.5 and −1.5 (n=638, mean +0.33%, t=1.58), against 48.5% after ordinary days (n=12,145).
findings.F3: After a large up day the next day rises less often than usual: 41.4% positive after a day above +2.5 standard deviations (n=319) and 44.9% after a day between +1.5 and +2.5 (n=691), against 48.5% after ordinary days, though the mean next-day excess is near zero (−0.08% and −0.03%).
findings.F4: Next-day excess return depends on the weekday of the bar: after Friday bars it is +0.30% (t=3.66, 51.7% positive, n=2,430) and after Thursday bars +0.21% (t=2.29), while after Wednesday bars it is −0.30% (t=−2.75) and after Monday bars −0.22% (t=−2.34).
findings.F5: The book's best and worst 1% of days (171 each, mean +27.7% and −22.5%) both come when the close sits far above its 200-day SMA (median distance 114% and 59%, against −1.5% on other days), with the forecast near its cap (19.7 and 15.1) and the trailing 20-day volatility near 0.079–0.080, against 0.042 on other days.
findings.F6: The distance above the 200-day SMA does not sort forward returns: across the ten distance deciles the 20-bar excess t-statistics all lie between −0.34 and 0.86, and on bars above the SMA only 42% of 20-bar returns beat the coin's mean.

ideas.idea: After a daily close that falls more than 1.5 times the coin's trailing 20-day standard deviation of daily returns, the next day's close is above that close more often than after ordinary days.
ideas.consequence: A trader could refuse to sell into, or take a long after, a large one-day drop for a one-day rebound.
ideas.name: one-day rebound after drops

ideas.idea: After a daily close that rises more than 1.5 times the coin's trailing 20-day standard deviation of daily returns, the next day's close is below that close more often than after ordinary days.
ideas.consequence: A trader could refuse to chase a new long on the close of a large up day.
ideas.name: next-day fade after spikes

ideas.idea: A coin's close-to-close return from Friday's daily close to Saturday's daily close is higher than its average daily return.
ideas.consequence: A trader could prefer to hold a coin over the Friday-to-Saturday bar and avoid adding on Wednesday closes.
ideas.name: Friday-into-Saturday crypto drift

ideas.idea: When a coin's close sits far above its 200-day SMA, its daily returns swing about twice as wide in both directions as when it sits near or below the average.
ideas.consequence: A trader could cut size when the close is far above the long average instead of adding on distance, as the forecast does.
ideas.name: stretched trends swing wider

ideas.idea: Once a coin's close moves above its 200-day SMA, it usually falls back below within a few days, and only a minority of these moves become long runs above the average.
ideas.consequence: A trader could refuse to treat a fresh close above the long average as an entry until it has held there for some days.
ideas.name: fresh crosses mostly whipsaw
